RFC 2859 · Proposal, not shipped

How the rows connect.

Five ways to tell Holistics which records belong together. Explained with tiny tables, not compiler internals.

Today, a relationship matches one column to another, with a unique record on the target side. This RFC lets the matching rule describe more of the real world.

Explore the examples5 examples · about 8 minutes

One ID isn’t always enough.

Composite key · P1

An order ships from two warehouses. To find the right shipment for an order line, match the order and the warehouse.

Same order ID AND same warehouse ID.
Find the shipment

Green + “Match” identifies the matching target row. Blue marks your selected source.

Without both columns

L1 matches both shipments for order 1042. The Saigon shipment does not belong to this Hanoi line.

With the proposed relationship

L1 matches only S1. No need to concatenate the two columns into a synthetic text key.

What you can do today

Create a combined order-and-warehouse key on both models, then relate those keys. Concatenation needs collision-safe encoding and consistent handling of missing values.

AML + ERD + SQL · composite key

Proposed RFC syntax, not released AML. These snippets define relationships only; the referenced models and dimensions must already exist.

Relationship order_line_shipment {
  type: 'many_to_one'

  on {
    from: r(order_lines.order_id)
    to:   r(shipments.order_id)
  }
  on {
    from: r(order_lines.warehouse_id)
    to:   r(shipments.warehouse_id)
  }
}

Each on block adds a column pair. Both must match. Here, warehouse_id represents the warehouse shown as Hanoi or Saigon in the sample.

SQL equivalent · match both columns

Illustrative row-level SQL, not an exact compiler output. A left join keeps order lines even when no shipment matches.

select
  l.id as line_id
  , l.order_id
  , l.warehouse_id
  , s.id as shipment_id
from order_lines as l
left join shipments as s
  on l.order_id = s.order_id
  and l.warehouse_id = s.warehouse_id;

For L1, the result is S1, not S2. Both equality conditions belong to the same join.

What must be true in the data?

The combination of order ID and warehouse ID must be unique in shipments for this many-to-one example. Neither column needs to be unique on its own. Composite keys are not a new cardinality type; they add more column pairs to a relationship.

Which record covered that date?

Range · P1

Maya moves from North campus to South campus on 1 April. An attendance record should use the campus she attended on that day.

Same student, with start ≤ attendance date < end.
Find the enrollment

Why not join on student ID alone?

Both enrollment versions have student ID 7. Joining only on that ID attaches the attendance to both campuses.

Try 1 April

The old enrollment ends exactly where the new one begins. Including the start and excluding the end gives one match, not two.

What you can do today

Put the student-and-date join in a SQL-based model. This centralizes the rule, but fixes the join in that model rather than declaring a reusable dataset relationship.

AML + ERD + SQL · range

Proposed RFC syntax, not released AML. Match the student first, then test the attendance date against the enrollment interval.

Relationship attendance_enrollment {
  type: 'range'

  on {
    from: r(attendance.student_id)
    to:   r(enrollments.student_id)
  }

  match: @aql
    attendance.attended_on >= enrollments.start_date
      and attendance.attended_on < enrollments.end_date
  ;;
}

>= includes the start; < excludes the end. On 1 April, only South campus matches. The @aql … ;; block contains the matching expression.

SQL equivalent · test the interval

Illustrative row-level SQL. All three conditions decide whether an enrollment matches; none removes an unmatched attendance row.

select
  a.student_id
  , a.attended_on
  , e.campus
from attendance as a
left join enrollments as e
  on a.student_id = e.student_id
  and a.attended_on >= e.start_date
  and a.attended_on < e.end_date;

31 March matches North; 1 April matches South. This uses explicit end dates, just like the sample. Overlapping intervals would still produce multiple matches.

Important assumption: ranges for the same student must not overlap. The proposed compiler does not check this; overlapping ranges can produce wrong totals.

What about a record with no end date?

The relationship must explicitly treat a missing end date as open-ended. A plain comparison with a missing value will not match. This example uses explicit dates to make the boundaries visible.

The ID matches. But the type doesn’t.

Relationship filters · P2

A comment can belong to a post or a photo. Both might have ID 42. The type tells us what 42 refers to.

Same target ID, but join to posts only when comment type = Post.
Follow a comment to its post

Without the type condition

“Great shot” incorrectly attaches to post 42, even though the comment belongs to photo 42.

With the relationship filter

The photo comment has no matched post. Under a left join, the comment remains; its post fields are empty.

What you can do today

Use a SQL-based model with the type check inside the left join to retain every comment. A report filter is simpler for post-only reporting, but removes other comment types from totals.

AML + ERD + SQL · relationship filter

Proposed RFC syntax, not released AML. The sample’s “Target ID” is commentable_id; “Type” is commentable_type.

Relationship comment_post {
  type: 'many_to_one'

  on {
    from: r(comments.commentable_id)
    to:   r(posts.id)
  }

  where {
    from: @aql comments.commentable_type == 'Post' ;;
  }
}

where.from constrains matches using the comments side only. Despite the name, the compiler puts this predicate in the SQL join condition, not a report-wide WHERE filter.

SQL equivalent · filter the match, not the report

Illustrative row-level SQL. Notice that the type check is inside on, not a trailing where.

select
  c.id as comment_id
  , c.commentable_type
  , p.id as post_id
  , p.title
from comments as c
left join posts as p
  on c.commentable_id = p.id
  and c.commentable_type = 'Post';

C2 remains in the result, with null post fields. Moving the type check into where would remove C2 entirely.

Why a relationship filter, not a dashboard filter?

A dashboard filter can remove the comment entirely. This rule instead decides whether a post matches. The RFC prefers a general, one-sided relationship filter over a dedicated “polymorphic” type.

The same feature can join to only the current customer version or only non-deleted products, without hiding historical or deleted records from every other relationship. A filter may reference one side of the relationship, not both.

One subscription. Several months.

Many-to-many condition · P2

To count active subscriptions by month, match each subscription to every month it overlaps. Several matches are the correct answer here.

Subscription start ≤ month end AND subscription end ≥ month start.
Find the active months
The report across all three subscriptions · active on at least one day
SubscriptionJanFebMarApr
AActiveActiveActive—
B—Active——
C——ActiveActive
Active subscriptions1221

Why “many-to-many”?

A subscription matches multiple months. A month matches multiple subscriptions. There is no unique “one” side.

What work does this remove?

For this case, you would not need a warehouse table that expands every subscription into daily rows just to connect it to calendar periods.

What you can do today

Build a warehouse table with one row per subscription and active month, then use ordinary equality relationships. It works, but adds rows and a transformation to maintain.

AML + ERD + SQL · many-to-many condition

Proposed RFC syntax, not released AML. Each subscription joins every reporting period its dates overlap.

Relationship subscription_period {
  type: 'many_to_many'
  from: r(subscriptions.id)
  to:   r(periods.label)

  match: @aql
    subscriptions.started_on <= periods.end_date
      and coalesce(subscriptions.ended_on, @9999-12-31)
        >= periods.start_date
  ;;
}

Here, from and to identify unique rows; they do not mean “subscription ID equals month label.” The match expression determines the pairs. Declare unique keys on both models. Use a year-qualified period label, such as 2026-01, not a repeating month name.

coalesce treats a missing subscription end as open-ended. The sample subscriptions all have explicit end dates.

SQL equivalent · count active subscriptions per month

This illustrative report starts from periods so months with no active subscriptions still appear. count(distinct s.id) counts each subscription once per month, not once per joined row.

select
  p.label as month
  , count(distinct s.id) as active_subscriptions
from periods as p
left join subscriptions as s
  on s.started_on <= p.end_date
  and (s.ended_on is null or s.ended_on >= p.start_date)
group by p.label
order by p.label;

The null check is equivalent to an open-ended subscription without a dialect-specific far-future date literal. January–April return 1, 2, 2, 1. This count-specific example is not the RFC’s general fan-out rewrite for sums and other measures.

Matching is not allocation. This counts active subscriptions; it does not prorate revenue by days. The monthly counts add to 6, but there are only 3 distinct subscriptions across the full period.

Use the rate from then, not now.

Point-in-time / ASOF · P3

You have a €100 order and a history of EUR→USD rates. Each rate has a start date, but no end date. Find the most recent rate on or before the order.

Same currency. Among rates starting on or before the order, pick the latest.
Price the €100 order in USD

Range asks “inside which interval?”

The target stores both start and end. Test whether the event falls inside. The proposed range type assumes intervals do not overlap.

ASOF asks “which boundary is closest?”

The target stores a boundary. Choose one applicable row using a closest-match rule. This example uses “starts at,” including the boundary date.

What you can do today

Compute each rate’s end date with lead in your transformation layer, then perform the range join in a SQL-based model. This needs upstream work but does not require native ASOF support.

AML + ERD + SQL · point-in-time / ASOF

Proposed RFC syntax, not released AML. This relationship chooses the rate row; a separate metric performs the currency conversion.

Relationship order_fx_rate {
  type: 'asof'

  on {
    from: r(orders.currency)
    to:   r(fx_rates.currency)
  }

  event_at:       r(orders.ordered_at)
  boundary_at:    r(fx_rates.valid_from)
  effective_rule: 'starts_at'
}

event_at is the order date. boundary_at is the rate’s effective-from date. starts_at selects the latest boundary on or before the event, including an exact-date match. All rates in this example convert into USD.

SQL equivalent · DuckDB / MotherDuck / ClickHouse

ASOF picks the nearest eligible rate, rather than every earlier rate. DuckDB and ClickHouse need asof left join to preserve unmatched orders.

select
  o.id as order_id
  , o.ordered_at
  , r.valid_from as rate_effective_from
  , r.rate
  , o.amount * r.rate as amount_usd
from orders as o
asof left join fx_rates as r
  on o.currency = r.currency
  and o.ordered_at >= r.valid_from;

For ClickHouse, use join_use_nulls = 1 if unmatched right-side fields must appear as null rather than type-default values. ClickHouse also restricts the supported join algorithms and match-column types.

SQL equivalent · Snowflake

Snowflake puts the date comparison in match_condition. Its asof join already preserves unmatched left-side rows.

select
  o.id as order_id
  , o.ordered_at
  , r.valid_from as rate_effective_from
  , r.rate
  , o.amount * r.rate as amount_usd
from orders as o
asof join fx_rates as r
  match_condition (o.ordered_at >= r.valid_from)
  on o.currency = r.currency;

For a €100 order on 1 March, the selected rate is 1.12 and the result is $112. An order before the first rate has no conversion. These are illustrative SQL forms, not support for ASOF on BigQuery.

Database limitation: the RFC proposes native ASOF support for Snowflake, ClickHouse, DuckDB and MotherDuck. BigQuery and the other non-native databases would not get this type in this version. Stored start/end ranges remain an alternative.

What is still tricky?

If two rates have the same currency and start date, the database may choose either one. The example avoids ties. The RFC prefers disallowing reverse two-way filtering for ASOF in this version.

ASOF is not always “latest before”: the proposal includes other boundary rules. This example deliberately teaches only the common “starts at” rule. A rate selected from the report period rather than the event date is a different requirement.

More matches must not mean inflated totals.

Connecting tables can repeat a record. Holistics must avoid counting the same source record twice within one report group.

Count orders by productWhy compiler work matters
Joined rows before duplicate protection
OrderLineProduct
O11Widget
O12Widget
O13Gadget
O21Widget
3 Widget rows after the join
2 actual Widget orders: O1 + O2

Count O1 once under Widget. O1 still counts once under Gadget too. Adding the two product counts gives 3, but the overall distinct order count is 2.

This protection already exists for supported relationships. The RFC proposes extending the query rewrite to new shapes that lack a simple equality key. It does not redefine sums or counts, and it does not make overlapping group totals additive.

SQL example · avoid counting an order twice

For this specific order-count report, count distinct order IDs inside each product group. This is an illustrative shortcut for a count, not the general compiler strategy.

select
  i.product
  , count(distinct o.id) as order_count
from orders as o
left join order_items as i
  on o.id = i.order_id
group by i.product;

Widget returns 2; Gadget returns 1. Do not replace a sum with sum(distinct amount): two different orders may have the same amount and both must count.

A modeling proposal, not a release note.

The benefit: express a business matching rule once in the semantic model, rather than repeat workarounds across metrics and reports.

Proposed priority and availability · as described in the RFC
PriorityCapabilityDatabase reach
P1Composite keys + rangeAll supported SQL dialects
P2Relationship filters + many-to-many conditionsAll supported SQL dialects
P3Point-in-time / ASOFNative ASOF databases only

Initial intent

A 15 September comment says the intended initial scope reaches P2. The page is WIP; no target app version is set. Priorities are not delivery dates.

Not settled here

UI work is deferred. Row-level permissions, pre-aggregation and persistence need separate analysis. Do not assume permission behavior is already solved.

Does this solve every many-to-many request?

No. The RFC does not propose a separate shortcut for joining repeated columns directly. Its general many-to-many condition can express equality, but shared-dimension reporting pitfalls remain. More expressive joins do not automatically make every report meaningful.

Based on RFC 2859: Support new relationship types, by Tan Huynh. Source read 22 September 2026. Examples are fictional teaching data, not customer records or a live Holistics query.
